title: The Message of the Sermon on the Mount
author: stott

entries.title: The Beatitudes: The Character of the Counter-Culture
entries.content_summary: Stott reads the Beatitudes not as eight separate personality types but as one balanced portrait of every citizen of God's kingdom. The 'blessing' is God's own approval, not a warm feeling, and it rests on qualities the world despises. To be 'poor in spirit' (5:3) is to confess spiritual bankruptcy -- that we have nothing to offer God and must receive everything as grace; this is where the kingdom begins. To 'hunger and thirst for righteousness' (5:6) is to crave both personal holiness and social justice with the appetite of the starving. To be 'pure in heart' (5:8) is to be single-minded and transparent, free of the duplicity that corrodes religion. Together they describe a people utterly unlike the self-confident, self-satisfied world around them -- the essence of what Stott calls the Christian counter-culture.
entries.content_detail:
Stott treats Matthew 5:3-12 as the introduction to the whole Sermon: a description of the people over whom God reigns, given before any of their conduct is spelled out. 'Blessed' is not a subjective feeling of happiness but an objective declaration -- God pronouncing these people approved and in the right. The striking thing, Stott stresses, is the sheer contrariness of the list: nearly every quality Jesus congratulates is one the surrounding culture pities or scorns.

To be 'poor in spirit' (5:3) is not to be financially destitute but to acknowledge our spiritual destitution -- that before God we are bankrupt, with no merit to plead and nothing to bring. Stott makes this the doorway to the kingdom, because only those who know they have nothing will receive the kingdom as a gift; it is the exact opposite of the self-reliance the world prizes. Mourning (5:4) follows naturally: a sorrow first over one's own sin, then over the world's.

To 'hunger and thirst for righteousness' (5:6) is to desire it with the raw urgency of the starving and parched. Characteristically, Stott refuses to narrow 'righteousness': it embraces righteousness of standing (justification), righteousness of character (holiness), and righteousness in society (justice). The disciple craves all three and is promised satisfaction.

To be 'pure in heart' (5:8) is to be single-minded and sincere -- undivided in devotion and free of the mixed motives and hypocrisy that infect religion. The promise, that they 'shall see God,' is the highest imaginable, reserved for the transparent.

Read together, Stott argues, the Beatitudes are not a menu of optional temperaments but a composite portrait of the one kingdom character to which every disciple is called, and the values by which that community stands over against both the godless world and merely nominal religion. This is what he means by a Christian counter-culture: a people whose beatitude is defined not by what they achieve but by what, in poverty of spirit, they receive.

entries.title: Salt and Light: The Christian Influence on Society
entries.content_summary: Stott takes salt and light as the two ways the counter-culture affects the world. Salt (5:13) is a preservative that hinders decay; light (5:16) positively illumines. The images assume a fundamental difference: society is dark and rotting, and Christians are to arrest its corruption and dispel its darkness precisely by being unlike it. Salt is useless once it loses its saltiness, and a lamp pointless when hidden -- so the church influences the world only so long as it keeps its distinctive character and stays visible. Stott presses the balance: Christian good works must be public enough to be seen ('let your light shine before men'), yet aimed not at self-advertisement but at glory redirected to the Father. Withdrawal into a holy huddle and worldly assimilation are the twin failures the metaphors rule out.
entries.content_detail:
In Matthew 5:13-16 Stott sees Jesus defining the disciples' relation to the wider world through two everyday metaphors. Salt and light are both useful, but they work in opposite directions: salt works negatively, checking decay, while light works positively, dispelling darkness. Both images carry a sober assumption about society -- that left to itself it tends toward rottenness and darkness. The Christian's task is not to imitate this decay but to counteract it.

Stott insists that the effectiveness of both depends on the Christian being distinct. Salt does its work only by remaining salt; if it loses its saltiness it is worthless, fit only to be thrown out and trodden underfoot. A lamp, likewise, is meant to be set on a stand, not hidden under a bowl; a concealed light is a contradiction in terms. The lesson he draws is pointed: the church affects the world only so far as it refuses to become like the world. Assimilation destroys influence as surely as saltless salt or a hidden lamp is useless.

At the same time, Stott resists any retreat into invisibility. The command is that our light should 'shine before others,' so that they may 'see your good works.' Christian influence is therefore not merely private and inward; it is meant to be seen -- a matter of visible good deeds in the public arena, consistent with Stott's lifelong insistence on the church's social responsibility. The safeguard against vanity is the last clause: the aim is that people, seeing the works, should 'glorify your Father in heaven,' not admire the doer. Good works are to be public in their visibility yet God-ward in their motive.

So the two images together map a whole posture toward society: neither escapist withdrawal nor comfortable conformity, but penetration -- a distinctive, visible people whose difference preserves and illumines the community they are set within, and whose goodness points beyond itself to God.

entries.title: A Greater Righteousness: Christ Fulfils the Law, Not Abolishes It
entries.content_summary: Against any notion that grace cancels God's moral demand, Stott expounds Jesus' insistence that he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfil them (5:17). The Old Testament is not repealed; it is brought to its intended completion in Christ and his teaching. From this follows the Sermon's programmatic verse: unless the disciples' righteousness surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees, they will never enter the kingdom (5:20). Stott is careful to define the surplus qualitatively, not quantitatively -- not more rules more scrupulously kept, but a deeper, inward righteousness of the heart that the Pharisees' external religion never reached. The antitheses that follow illustrate exactly this: Jesus does not relax the commandments but radicalizes them, driving them past outward conformity to inward reality.
entries.content_detail:
Matthew 5:17-20 functions for Stott as the hinge between the Beatitudes and the specific ethical teaching that follows, and as a decisive statement about the disciple's relation to the Old Testament. Jesus flatly denies any intention to abolish the Law and the Prophets; he has come to 'fulfil' them. Stott unpacks 'fulfil' broadly: Jesus brings the law to its intended completion by obeying it, by driving it to its full and deep meaning, and by embodying the reality to which its types and prophecies pointed. The Scriptures are not discarded but honoured and consummated in him.

The permanence of God's moral standard is underscored by the saying that not the smallest letter or stroke will pass from the law until all is accomplished (5:18). Stott uses this to warn against antinomianism -- the assumption that Christian liberty means freedom from God's righteous demands. The kingdom does not lower the ethical bar; it raises it.

Hence verse 20, which Stott treats as programmatic for the rest of chapter 5: the disciples' righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, or they will not enter the kingdom at all. The crucial question is how it exceeds. Stott argues the difference is one of kind, not merely of degree. Pharisaic righteousness was external, concerned with the outward act and the letter of regulation, and it was fatally shallow because it left the heart untouched. The greater righteousness Jesus requires reaches inward to motive, desire, and attitude; it is a matter of the heart before it is a matter of the hand.

Stott thus positions the Sermon between two errors it equally rejects: the pharisaism that reduces righteousness to external performance, and the antinomianism that dispenses with righteousness altogether. The antitheses of 5:21 onward are, on his reading, six worked examples of this same principle -- Jesus taking commandments the tradition had shrunk to outward observance and restoring their full, heart-searching depth.

entries.title: Murder and Adultery in the Heart: Righteousness Made Inward
entries.content_summary: In the first two antitheses Stott shows Jesus taking the commandments against murder and adultery and pressing them back to their root in the heart. The contrast ('you have heard... but I say') is not between Jesus and Moses, but between Jesus and the scribal tradition that had shrunk God's law to external acts. Unjust anger and the contemptuous word already breach the sixth commandment (5:22); the lustful look already breaches the seventh (5:28). Sin is thus located in attitude and imagination, not merely in deed, so no one can claim innocence on the ground of outward respectability. The drastic sayings about the eye and the hand (5:29-30) are Stott's vivid case for ruthless self-discipline: whatever feeds sin must be dealt with decisively, though the surgery he intends is moral, not literal.
entries.content_detail:
Stott reads the six 'antitheses' as Jesus' own illustrations of the greater righteousness of 5:20, and he is emphatic on one point of interpretation: the formula 'You have heard that it was said... but I say to you' does not pit Jesus against Moses. Jesus is not correcting the Old Testament; he is correcting the scribal misinterpretations of it that had reduced God's commandments to a matter of external observance. His quarrel is with the tradition, not with the text.

In the first antithesis Jesus reaches behind the act of murder to the anger and contempt that fuel it. To nurse unjust anger against a brother, or to spit out the contemptuous insult, already places a person under judgment (5:22), because it is the same murderous disposition that the sixth commandment forbids. Stott notes the corollary Jesus draws: reconciliation takes priority even over worship, so that one should leave the gift at the altar and first be reconciled (5:24). The command is not merely to avoid killing but to pursue peace.

In the second antithesis Jesus reaches behind the act of adultery to the lustful look and the cultivated fantasy: to look at another 'with lustful intent' is already to commit adultery in the heart (5:28). Sin is thus traced to the imagination and the will, not confined to the body's deed. This is precisely the inwardness that makes the disciple's righteousness exceed the Pharisees'.

The hard sayings about tearing out the eye and cutting off the hand (5:29-30) follow as Jesus' call to drastic action. Stott is clear that Jesus is not commanding literal mutilation but demanding a ruthless moral discipline -- a readiness to renounce whatever occasions sin, however precious it feels, because the stakes are the whole self. Taken together, the two antitheses show that the kingdom's righteousness is a matter of the heart's disposition, exposing sin where mere respectability had concealed it and refusing the comfort of a merely external innocence.

entries.title: Non-Retaliation and Love of Enemies: The Measure Is the Father
entries.chapter_or_episode: Matthew 5:38-48 -- retaliation and love of enemies
entries.content_summary: Stott reads the last two antitheses as the summit of the Sermon's counter-culture. Jesus forbids personal retaliation (5:39) -- not the abolition of justice or the courts, but the renunciation of private revenge and a readiness to absorb insult and go the second mile. He then demolishes the 'love neighbour, hate enemy' formula the tradition had built, commanding love even of enemies and prayer for persecutors (5:44). The ground is theological, not sentimental: God sends sun and rain on just and unjust alike, and his children are to reflect that indiscriminate generosity. To love only those who love us is merely to match the tax collectors; the disciple is called to a love without boundary, summed up in the call to be 'perfect' -- that is, all-embracing in love -- as the heavenly Father is (5:48).
entries.content_detail:
The fifth and sixth antitheses, Stott argues, carry the Sermon's ethic to its most demanding and most distinctive point. In the matter of retaliation, Jesus cites the 'eye for eye' principle (5:38). Stott observes that this lex talionis was originally a merciful limit on vengeance and a rule for the courts, restricting punishment to fit the crime. The scribes had twisted it into a licence for personal revenge. Jesus forbids that private retaliation altogether. The four vivid illustrations -- turning the other cheek, surrendering the cloak as well as the tunic, going the second mile, giving to the one who asks -- are not, on Stott's reading, a naive abolition of law, order, or justice, but a portrait of a heart so free of vindictiveness that it will rather suffer wrong and overflow in generosity than insist on its rights.

The climax is the command to love enemies and pray for persecutors (5:44). Stott stresses that the tradition's addition, 'and hate your enemy,' appears nowhere in the law; Jesus strips it away and extends neighbour-love to its widest possible reach. The motive he gives is imitation of God: the Father 'makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.' Since God's generosity is indiscriminate, his children's love must be too. To love only those who love us, Jesus points out, is no achievement at all -- even tax collectors and pagans manage that. The distinctive mark of the kingdom is love that reaches the undeserving and the hostile.

Stott interprets the concluding command, 'be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect' (5:48), not as a demand for flawless sinlessness but, in context, as a summons to the completeness and maturity of love -- a love as all-embracing as God's own. Here, he says, is the height of the Christian counter-culture: a community whose love has no natural boundary because it mirrors the character of the Father himself.

entries.title: Devotion for God's Eyes: Giving, Praying, Fasting, and the Lord's Prayer
entries.chapter_or_episode: Matthew 6:1-18 -- secret piety and the pattern prayer
entries.content_summary: Turning from conduct toward others to devotion toward God, Stott shows Jesus attacking the great religious temptation: performing piety to be admired. Giving, prayer, and fasting are each to be done in secret, 'seen' only by the Father who sees in secret (6:6), because an audience of one is the death of hypocrisy and the birth of sincerity. Christian prayer avoids both the ostentation of the hypocrite and the mechanical babbling of the pagan; God already knows our needs, so prayer is the trusting approach of children, not the manipulation of a reluctant deity. In the Lord's Prayer (6:9) Stott finds the model of right priorities: God's name, kingdom, and will come first, and only then our bread, forgiveness, and deliverance -- the whole ordered by the intimate address 'Our Father.'
entries.content_detail:
Having dealt with the disciple's righteousness toward other people, Stott notes that in Matthew 6 Jesus turns to the disciple's righteousness toward God -- the realm of religious devotion. The governing warning is against practising piety 'to be seen by others.' Jesus takes the three classic acts of Jewish devotion -- almsgiving, prayer, and fasting -- and in each case exposes the same danger and prescribes the same remedy. The hypocrites parade their giving, praying, and fasting for a human audience, and Stott presses Jesus' verdict: they have their reward in full, the applause they sought and nothing more. The disciple, by contrast, is to give, pray, and fast in secret, before the Father 'who sees in secret' (6:6). The point is not that piety must be invisible for its own sake but that its true audience is God alone; when we no longer perform for people, sincerity becomes possible.

Stott then distinguishes Christian prayer from two counterfeits. It is unlike the hypocrite's prayer, which is really self-display; and it is unlike the pagan's 'empty phrases,' the heaping up of words as though God must be worn down or informed. Since the Father already knows our needs before we ask, prayer is not the manipulation of a reluctant deity but the confident approach of children to a Father who delights to give.

Against that backdrop Stott expounds the Lord's Prayer (6:9-13) as the model of rightly ordered prayer. It opens with the relationship, 'Our Father in heaven' -- intimacy and reverence held together. Its first three petitions are God-centred: that his name be hallowed, his kingdom come, his will be done. Only then do the human petitions follow -- daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil. Stott draws out the sequence as a lesson in priorities: God's glory and cause come before our needs. He also highlights the sobering reciprocity attached to forgiveness (6:12, 6:14-15) -- those who will not forgive others cannot expect to be forgiven, because an unforgiving spirit shows that grace has not truly been received. Throughout, the Fatherhood of God frames the whole: devotion is the family life of God's children, lived for his eyes.

entries.title: God or Mammon: Undivided Loyalty and Freedom from Anxiety
entries.content_summary: Stott presents the choice of two masters as unavoidable: 'You cannot serve God and mammon' (6:24). Money is not neutral once it becomes a rival god; the heart follows its treasure, so the disciple lays up treasure in heaven rather than on earth. From this settled loyalty flows freedom from anxiety. Stott stresses that Jesus does not commend carelessness but forbids corrosive worry, and does so by appeal to the Father's providence: if God feeds the birds and clothes the grass, his children need not be paralyzed by fear over food and clothing. Worry is, at bottom, a failure of faith and a pagan preoccupation. The positive command reorders everything -- 'seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness' (6:33) -- and the necessities will be supplied as by-products of that single-minded pursuit.
entries.content_detail:
In Matthew 6:19-34 Stott sees Jesus addressing the disciple's relation to material possessions, and he treats the passage as a unity built around one decisive either/or. The heart, Jesus says, follows its treasure: where you store your wealth, there your affections will settle (6:21). So the disciple is to lay up treasure in heaven rather than on earth, choosing durable, eternal riches over perishable ones. Between these two lies no neutral ground. 'No one can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and mammon' (6:24). Stott underlines that mammon -- money and material security -- is not a harmless servant but a would-be rival god, demanding a devotion that belongs to God alone. Loyalty must be single and undivided.

From this settled loyalty Stott derives the passage's second theme: freedom from anxiety. He is careful to say that Jesus is not commending an irresponsible carelessness about work or provision; he is forbidding the corroding worry that betrays a lack of trust. Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: God feeds the birds, who neither sow nor reap, and clothes the wild flowers, which are here today and gone tomorrow -- how much more will he provide for his own children? To be consumed with anxiety over food, drink, and clothing is, Jesus says, to behave like the pagans who do not know the Father; it is, in effect, practical unbelief.

The cure Stott highlights is not merely the removal of worry but its replacement by a new and overriding ambition: 'Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you' (6:33). The disciple who makes God's rule and God's righteousness the first priority discovers that the necessities of life are supplied as by-products of that single-minded pursuit. Anxiety and the divided heart are thus answered by the same remedy -- a wholehearted, trusting orientation toward God, which Stott presents as another facet of the counter-culture: a community freed from the money-worship and the fretful insecurity that drive the surrounding world.

entries.title: Do Not Judge: Against the Censorious Spirit
entries.content_summary: Stott is careful not to let 'Judge not' (7:1) be misread as a ban on all moral discernment -- the same passage warns against dogs and swine, and false prophets follow soon after, both of which require judgment. What Jesus forbids is the censorious, fault-finding spirit that presumes to play God over others while excusing itself. The comedy of the speck and the plank (7:3-5) exposes the hypocrite who fusses over a splinter in a brother's eye while a great beam juts from his own; self-examination must come first, and only then is the disciple fit to help remove the brother's speck. Stott thus holds together two truths the world keeps splitting apart: Christians are to be neither harsh, presumptuous critics nor undiscerning sentimentalists, but humble, clear-sighted people who judge themselves before assessing anyone else.
entries.content_detail:
Stott approaches 'Judge not, that you be not judged' (7:1) by first clearing away a common misreading. The verse cannot be an absolute prohibition of all evaluation, for two reasons drawn from its immediate context. In verse 6 Jesus tells his disciples not to give what is holy to 'dogs' or to throw pearls before 'swine,' which requires a discriminating judgment about people; and a few verses later he commands them to beware of false prophets and to test them 'by their fruits' (7:15-20), which is impossible without discernment. So Jesus is not forbidding the exercise of a critical faculty as such.

What he forbids, Stott argues, is being censorious -- the harsh, fault-finding, condemning spirit that sets itself up as judge over others. This is a usurpation of God's prerogative, for God alone is the true Judge, and it is invariably marked by a double standard: severe toward others, indulgent toward oneself. Jesus warns that the measure we use will be measured back to us (7:2); the censorious invite the very judgment they hand out.

The famous illustration of the speck and the plank (7:3-5) drives the point home with deliberate absurdity. The critic obsesses over a tiny splinter in his brother's eye while a whole plank protrudes from his own -- and is so blinded by it that he cannot even see straight to perform the delicate operation he presumes to offer. Stott notes that Jesus does not forbid helping a brother remove the speck; he insists only on the right order. First deal drastically with the plank in your own eye -- that is, honest and humbling self-examination and self-judgment -- and then you will 'see clearly' to help your brother.

Stott thus refuses both extremes. The disciple is not to be a harsh, hypocritical critic, nor a flabby sentimentalist who has abandoned all moral discrimination. The kingdom character is humility that judges itself first, joined to a clear-sighted love that can then help others -- discernment purged of the censoriousness that so easily counterfeits it.

entries.title: The Sermon's Great Divide: Two Ways, Two Trees, Two Builders
entries.content_summary: Stott reads the Sermon's ending as a series of stark either/ors that press for decision. There are two gates and two ways (7:13-14): the broad road that many travel to destruction, and the narrow one, hard to find, that leads to life. There are two kinds of teacher, to be tested by their fruit, since not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter, but only the one who does the Father's will (7:21) -- profession without obedience is worthless and self-deceiving. And there are two builders (7:24): the wise who hears Jesus' words and does them, founded on rock, and the foolish who hears and does nothing, built on sand. When the storm comes the difference between hearing and doing proves total. The counter-culture, Stott concludes, is entered only by a deliberate, obedient commitment.
entries.content_detail:
Stott treats Matthew 7:13-27 as the deliberate conclusion of the whole Sermon, in which Jesus stops describing the kingdom life and demands a response to it. The rhetoric turns to a series of sharp alternatives, each pressing the hearer to choose.

First come the two ways (7:13-14). There is a wide gate opening onto an easy, spacious road that 'many' travel, and it ends in destruction; and there is a narrow gate opening onto a hard road that 'few' find, and it leads to life. Stott notes the deliberate discomfort of this: the popular, crowded path is not thereby the safe one, and entering the kingdom requires a definite decision to turn aside onto the harder, less-travelled road.

Second come the two kinds of teacher (7:15-20), the false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are inwardly ravenous wolves. They are to be recognized 'by their fruits,' since a tree is known by what it produces. Stott stresses that Jesus expects his disciples to discriminate -- an echo of the discernment presupposed earlier -- rather than to be naive about those who mislead.

Third, and closely joined, is the warning that profession is not the same as reality (7:21-23). Not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom, but only the one 'who does the will of my Father.' Stott presses the sobering scene of those who claim impressive works in Jesus' name yet hear, 'I never knew you.' Words, orthodoxy, even apparent power are no substitute for obedience and a real relationship with Christ.

Finally come the two builders (7:24-27), which Stott sees as gathering up the whole. The wise builder hears Jesus' words 'and does them,' and so builds on rock; the foolish builder hears the same words and does nothing, building on sand. Both face the same storm, but only the house on rock stands. The decisive line runs between hearing and doing. So the Sermon ends, Stott concludes, not with admiration but with a summons: the counter-culture is entered and sustained only by those who translate Christ's teaching into obedient action.
